name: AI for Team Sports
objectives: Given your team's identity, choose three to five team stats and write a clear definition for each, with every stat collectable every game and a person assigned to collect it

Using Google Sheets, set up a shared team stats sheet with a summary tab and safe access, with edit access only for staff who collect, view-only for others, never public, and no medical, grade or contact information

Given stats from at least three games or practices, identify one lineup or play pattern using sorting, filters or an AI assistant, with player numbers or initials only, the AI's math checked, and small samples treated as questions

Given public results and allowed film of a real opponent, write a one-page scouting summary of their offense, defense, key players and three keys to beat them, with every point from your own notes and league scouting rules followed

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing team stats that matter
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick three to five team stats tied to how your team wants to play.
This lesson builds toward: Given your team's identity, you will choose three to five team stats and write a clear definition for each, with every stat collectable every game and a person assigned to collect it.
Team analytics starts with your team's identity. A fast-break basketball team cares about transition points and turnovers. A possession soccer team cares about completed passes and shots from the box. A volleyball team cares about serve receive and side-out percentage.
Pick three to five stats you can actually collect every game with the people you have: a manager, a parent volunteer, an injured player, or video afterward.
Write a clear definition for each so everyone counts it the same way: "A turnover is any possession lost without a shot."
Step by step:
- Write your team's identity in one sentence.
- List stats that match it.
- Pick three to five you can collect every game.
- Write a clear definition for each.
- Assign who collects them.
Words to know:
- Team analytics: using numbers about a team to understand and improve how it plays.
- Definition: a clear rule for exactly what counts.
Try it now: Write your team's identity in one sentence. Ask an AI assistant to suggest stats that match it, then pick three to five and write definitions.
You can now choose and define team stats that match how your team plays.

check.q: Which stats fit a possession soccer team?
options: Completed passes and shots from the box
check.why: Stats should match how your team wants to play.

check.q: Two volunteers count turnovers differently. What do you do?
options: Let each count their own way
Write one clear definition everyone uses
check.why: A clear definition makes everyone count the same way.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: A shared team stats sheet
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a shared Google Sheet for team stats with safe access.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets, you will set up a shared team stats sheet with a summary tab and safe access, with edit access only for staff who collect, view-only for others, never public, and no medical, grade or contact information.
Use one Google Sheet with a tab per game, or one long table with columns: Date, Opponent, Quarter or Set, Lineup, and your stats. A summary tab can total the season.
Share it only with the coaching staff and managers who need to edit. Use view-only links for others, and never make a sheet with player information public on the web.
Keep only game stats in this sheet. Do not put medical notes, grades, family information or contact details in a team stats sheet; those belong in your school's official systems with the right privacy protections.
Step by step:
- Create a Google Sheet with clear columns.
- Add a summary tab for season totals.
- Share edit access only with staff who collect.
- Use view-only for others; never public.
- Keep medical, grades and contact info out.
Words to know:
- Shared sheet: a spreadsheet several people can open, with access you control.
- View-only: people can see but cannot change it.
Try it now: Create your team stats sheet, enter one past game from memory or a box score, and check the sharing settings.
You can now set up a shared team stats sheet with safe access.

check.q: What does a summary tab in the team sheet do?
check.why: A summary tab can total the season from each game.

check.q: A parent asks for the team stats sheet link. What do you share?
options: A view-only link, if your rules allow it
The whole folder with medical notes
check.why: Use view-only for people who do not collect, and never make it public.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding lineup and play patterns
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use your sheet and an AI assistant to spot one lineup or play pattern.
This lesson builds toward: Given stats from at least three games or practices, you will identify one lineup or play pattern using sorting, filters or an AI assistant, with player numbers or initials only, the AI's math checked, and small samples treated as questions.
After a few games, look for patterns: Which lineups are outscoring opponents? Which quarter or set do we struggle in? Which play type leads to the most points?
Use sorting, filters or a pivot table in Google Sheets. Or copy the table (with player initials or numbers instead of full names) into an AI assistant and ask: "Which lineups have the best point difference? Which period is weakest? Show your math." Check its math against the sheet.
Small samples mislead. A lineup that played four minutes is not proven. Treat patterns as questions for practice and film, not final answers, and the coach decides.
Step by step:
- Sort or filter by lineup and period.
- Use player numbers or initials, not full names, with AI.
- Ask AI to find patterns and show its math.
- Check its math.
- Turn one pattern into a question for practice or film.
Words to know:
- Point differential: points scored minus points allowed.
- Pivot table: a spreadsheet tool that groups and totals data, like points by lineup.
- Sample size: how much data you have; small samples can mislead.
Try it now: Enter at least two games in your sheet. Ask an AI assistant to find the best and worst period or lineup and show its math. Check it and write one question for practice.
You can now find lineup and play patterns and treat them as questions for the coach.

check.q: What should you ask AI to do along with finding lineup patterns?
check.why: Ask AI to show its math so you can check it against the sheet.

check.q: Your third period is weak in every game so far. What do you do with this pattern?
options: Take it to practice and film as a question for the coach
check.why: Treat patterns as questions for practice and film; the coach decides.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Scouting an opponent with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page opponent scouting summary from public information.
This lesson builds toward: Given public results and allowed film of a real opponent, you will write a one-page scouting summary of their offense, defense, key players and three keys to beat them, with every point from your own notes and league scouting rules followed.
Scouting means learning how an opponent plays before you face them. Use public sources: past results, published box scores, league stats pages, and game film your team has or that is publicly posted. Follow your league's rules on film exchange and scouting.
Watch with three questions: What do they do most on offense? What do they do most on defense? Who are their key players, and what do those players like to do?
Paste your notes into an AI assistant and ask: "Turn these scouting notes into a one-page summary: their offense, defense, key players, three keys to beat them. Short bullets." Check that every point came from your notes, not the AI's guesses.
Step by step:
- Collect public results, stats and allowed film.
- Watch with three questions.
- Write notes with timestamps.
- Ask AI for a one-page summary from your notes only.
- Check every bullet against your notes.
Words to know:
- Scouting report: a summary of how an opponent plays and how to beat them.
- Tendency: something a team or player does often in a certain situation.
Try it now: Pick a real upcoming opponent. Gather public info, write notes with three questions, and use AI to make a one-page summary. Check every bullet.
You can now write a one-page opponent scouting summary from public sources with AI help.

check.q: Which is one of the three scouting questions?
options: What do they do most on offense?
How many fans do they have?
check.why: Watch for offense, defense and key players.

check.q: You want film of an opponent that is not public. What do you do?
options: Ask a friend on their team to send it
Follow your league's film exchange rules
Use AI to guess what they do
check.why: Follow your league's rules on film exchange and scouting.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Clear team communication
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn data and scouting into short, clear team messages.
This lesson builds toward: Given your data and scouting summary, you will write a short team message with one to three key points, sent through the approved team channel, with individual feedback kept private.
Players don't need every number. They need one to three clear points: "They press after every made basket. Inbound to the middle." Short messages stick.
Use AI to turn your summary into different versions: a 30-second talk for the locker room, a one-slide graphic for film session, and a short message for the team's official communication app. Match your school's rules on how coaches contact players, especially minors.
Praise in public, correct in private. Team messages talk about the team, not one player's mistakes.
Step by step:
- Pick one to three key points.
- Ask AI for a 30-second talk, one slide and a short message.
- Send through your team's official channel.
- Keep individual feedback private.
Words to know:
- Key point: the one thing players must remember.
- Official channel: the communication method your school or club approves for team messages.
Try it now: Take your scouting summary and use AI to make a 30-second talk and a three-sentence team message with no more than three key points.
You can now turn data into short, clear and respectful team messages.

check.q: What do players need from a team message?
check.why: Short messages with a few clear points stick.

check.q: One player keeps making the same mistake. How do you address it?
options: Call it out in the team chat
Post it on the team page
Show it on the film session slide
Talk with the player in private
check.why: Praise in public, correct in private.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Privacy and fairness in team data
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set team data rules that protect players and keep decisions fair.
This lesson builds toward: For your team's data, you will write team data rules that protect player privacy and keep decisions fair, covering what to collect, where to store it, what never goes into AI, who approves apps, and how decisions are explained to players.
Player data is personal. Stats, video, and especially health, wearable and academic information need care. Collect only what you need, keep it in approved places, and delete what you no longer need according to your school's rules.
Do not paste full names, health information or private details into AI tools. Use numbers or initials. Many schools and leagues have rules about student data and approved apps; ask your athletic director.
Fairness: numbers can miss things like effort, leadership or defense that doesn't show in a box score, and small samples can be unfair to bench players. Use data to ask better questions, and explain decisions to players as people.
Step by step:
- Collect only what you need.
- Store it in approved places.
- Use numbers or initials with AI.
- Ask your athletic director about data and app rules.
- Explain decisions to players as people.
Words to know:
- Student data: information about students, which schools must protect.
- Bias: unfairness that can come from incomplete data or assumptions.
Try it now: Final task: write five team data rules, then finish your stats sheet, one pattern, your one-page scouting summary and a team message that protects player privacy.
You can now use team data in a way that protects players and keeps decisions fair.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Stats sheet Fewer than three games, unclear stats, or unsafe sharing or private data in the sheet. Three to five defined stats for three games or practices, a summary tab and safe, role-based access. A person is assigned for each stat and the definitions are on a tab everyone can read. Pattern found No pattern, AI math unchecked, or full names used with AI. One lineup or play pattern with checked math, using numbers or initials only. Notes the sample size and turns the pattern into a practice or film question for the coach. Scouting summary Points that did not come from notes, or sources outside league rules. One page with offense, defense, key players and three keys, every point from the learner's notes and allowed sources. Includes timestamps that show each key point. Team message and privacy Too many points, or a player's mistake or private information is shared. One to three key points sent through the approved channel with no private player information. Versions for a locker room talk, a slide and a message, all respecting privacy. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should you do with player data you no longer need?
options: Delete it according to your school's rules
check.why: Collect only what you need and delete what you no longer need by your school's rules.

check.q: A bench player has poor numbers from only six minutes played. What is fair?
options: Treat the small sample with care and talk with them as a person
check.why: Small samples can be unfair to bench players; explain decisions to players as people.
